The Hatch Act is a federal law that regulates the partisan political activities of most executive-branch employees, excluding the President and Vice President. As amended in 1993, the Hatch Act exempts some high-level administration officials from some of its prohibitions, allowing them to engage in certain political activities while on duty. This exemption applies to certain officials appointed by the President with Senate confirmation (PAS), and some high-level political officials who are paid from an appropriation for the Executive Office of the President (EOP). Other Hatch Act provisions, however, continue to limit the political activities of these officials. This In Focus provides an overview of the law as it applies to certain high-level administration officials, including Cabinet Secretaries.
The Hatch Act: Background
The Hatch Act, enacted in 1939, was designed to address concerns regarding political patronage in the civil service. The underlying rationale for the law is that “efficiency in Government service requires a lack of partisanship in administration.” In its current form, the law regulates the partisan political activity of covered employees, which includes nearly all federal civilian executive-branch employees, but exempts from its coverage the President and Vice President. The U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC) renders advisory opinions concerning the Hatch Act and is authorized to investigate and pursue sanctions for alleged violations of the law.
More information about the Hatch Act and its coverage is available in another In Focus. Two key provisions are relevant when discussing the Hatch Act’s application to high-level administration officials. First, the Hatch Act prohibits a covered employee from engaging in political activity while the employee is on duty, in a federal building, wearing an official uniform, or using any government vehicle. Certain high-level officials, however, are exempt from this prohibition. Second, the Hatch Act prohibits all covered employees from using their “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election.”
On-Duty Prohibition
Among other things, the Hatch Act prohibits covered employees from engaging in political activity while on duty, in the federal workplace, in uniform, or in a vehicle owned or leased by the federal government. Political activity is defined in regulation as “an activity directed toward the success or failure of a political party, candidates for partisan political office, or partisan political group.”
The Hatch Act, however, exempts from this prohibition certain employees who are deemed to be on duty at all times, and who are either paid from an EOP appropriation or are PAS employees. The exemption for PAS employees applies only to one “whose position is located within the United States and who determines policies to be pursued by the United States in relations with foreign powers or in the nationwide administration of Federal laws.” Legislative history suggests that this exemption was intended to apply to “high-level political officials” who are continuously on duty and otherwise could never engage in political activity. OSC has referred to exemptions in the Annual and Sick Leave Act to help determine which employees are considered on duty at all times.
Employees exempted from the Hatch Act’s on-duty prohibitions may engage in political activity, but costs associated with that activity may not be paid for with money derived from the Treasury. The Treasury must be reimbursed for costs associated with political activity “within a reasonable period of time,” and Hatch Act regulations provide guidance on how officials must apportion costs of travel that includes both official and political events. OSC recommends that agencies seek reimbursement for political activity within 30 days of the event. Reimbursement may be sought from a campaign or from officials themselves.
Official-Authority Prohibition
High-level administration officials who are allowed to engage in political activity on duty must abide by another Hatch Act provision prohibiting all covered employees from using their “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election.” OSC has explained that this prohibition exists because “using an official title in connection with one’s political activity . . . risks implying that the government itself has a preference for one political party or candidate over another.”
Issues regarding the official-authority prohibition may arise when high-level administration officials mix political activities with official work, such as by using an official title when participating in political activity. OSC has indicated that it can be challenging to distinguish permissible official activity from prohibited political activity, as political activity may encompass more than just “express advocacy for the electoral success or failure of a candidate.” OSC has offered some examples of comments that employees are “unquestionably” prohibited from making while engaged in official duties. These include 
attacking the campaign of a candidate for partisan political office, 
explaining why voters should support a particular candidate, 
comparing campaign proposals, or
forecasting what would happen if certain candidates were elected. 
As one example of improper use of official authority, OSC found a high-level official violated the Hatch Act when he participated in an interview in his official capacity and suggested that one candidate’s proposals would negatively affect the federal program the official oversaw.
The official-authority prohibition may also be implicated if a high-level administration official attends an event in his or her official authority while engaging in campaign-related activity. OSC has advised that when officials speak in a personal capacity for a political purpose, they must “avoid talking about the work of their agencies to ensure that they do not mix their official work with their personal political activity.” For example, OSC concluded that a Cabinet Secretary violated the Hatch Act when she attended an event to speak about administration policies, but endorsed a candidate for partisan political office at the event. While the Secretary was permitted to attend the political event and engage in political activity, she was prohibited from doing so in her official capacity. 
In the same vein, covered employees, including high-level administration officials, are prohibited from organizing official events for the purpose of promoting or supporting a candidate, a partisan political group, or a political party. In one instance, OSC determined that an Acting Secretary violated the Hatch Act when he presided over an official event that was held for the purpose of creating content for a political party convention.
The official-authority provision of the Hatch Act also prohibits all covered employees, including high-level officials, from taking official actions for the purpose of promoting a candidate’s campaign for partisan political office. For example, OSC determined that a Cabinet Secretary violated the Hatch Act when he authorized a change to agency rules to allow himself to address a political convention to promote a candidate’s reelection campaign. OSC also found a Hatch Act violation when a high-level administration official released nonpublic official information to help a candidate’s campaign.
Official Versus Political Events
While some high-level officials may engage in on-duty political activity—such as attending political events—in their personal capacity, it is not always clear when an event is considered official versus political for purposes of determining Treasury reimbursement.
As a hypothetical example, a Cabinet Secretary may be invited to attend an event to promote agency work hosted by a sitting Member of Congress who is up for reelection. If the event is considered political or is part of a trip that involves both official and political events, the Hatch Act requires that the Cabinet Secretary reimburse the Treasury for any time spent on political activity. The Cabinet Secretary is also prohibited from using their official title while engaging in the activity.
OSC has identified multiple, non-exclusive factors to consider when determining whether an event is political for purposes of the Hatch Act. The factors outlined in an OSC advisory opinion include inquiries into
the type of event, 
the speakers at the event and the intended audience,
the organizers of the event,
the relationship between the event and official agency business,
whether candidates (including incumbents seeking reelection) will be present at the event, 
the proximity of the event to the date of an election,
the frequency of similar types of events during non-election years, 
who invited the official to speak, 
the official’s motivation for attending the event,
whether the event was scheduled prior to any candidate involvement,
whether the event is open or closed to the media, and
the content of the event speakers’ remarks.
OSC advises that these factors “are intended to help determine whether the official aspect of an event is bona fide or merely a pretext for helping a candidate or political party.” 
Enforcement and Remedies
Multiple agencies are responsible for interpreting, implementing, and imposing penalties under the Act. As mentioned, OSC renders advisory opinions concerning the law and is authorized to investigate and pursue sanctions for alleged violations before the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), a body that oversees disputes arising from the federal workforce. The MSPB then determines whether a violation has occurred and imposes available penalties, which, for federal employees, can include disciplinary action such as removal; a reduction in grade; debarment from federal employment for a period not to exceed five years; suspension; reprimand; or civil fines. 
Some unique challenges may arise when high-level administration officials violate the Hatch Act. For example, if an alleged violation involves an “employee in a confidential, policymaking, policy-determining, or policy-advocating position appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate,” a complaint must be presented to the President for “appropriate action” in lieu of being presented to the MSPB. OSC also refers complaints involving White House commissioned officers to the President and has no role in disciplining PAS employees or White House commissioned officers beyond issuing a report. Thus, for example, if a high-level official participates in political activity on duty and fails to reimburse the Treasury, OSC lacks authority to pursue corrective action and cannot recover costs unless the employee voluntarily agrees to facilitate reimbursement.

Conflict is spreading in Ethiopia, where eight opposition groups have formed an armed alliance against the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and the country may be heading toward war with neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia’s overlapping rebellions and its mounting tensions—not only with Eritrea but also with Egypt and Sudan—threaten to spur a broader regional conflict in which Middle East powers could take sides. 
The governments of Ethiopia and Eritrea have traded allegations for over a year: Eritrea asserts that Ethiopia—landlocked since Eritrea became independent in 1993—seeks war as a pretext to forcefully acquire sovereign access to the sea, and Ethiopia has accused Eritrea (and Egypt) of waging a proxy conflict through rebel groups. U.S. officials have sought to defuse tensions, but both Ethiopia and Eritrea appear to be preparing for war.
Congress was active on Ethiopia during the deadly 2020-2022 war in northern Ethiopia, and some Members of Congress have since expressed concern about human rights abuses, tensions with Eritrea, and the prospect of another conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. Several Members have expressed alarm over the conflict and called for deescalation.   
The Horn of Africa is home to several of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, including the largest, in neighboring Sudan, and the situation in Ethiopia threatens to further strain an aid system stretched by aid cuts and competing crises. At a time when the Red Sea region already faces threats emanating from the war in Yemen, a war between Ethiopia—Africa’s second most populous country—and Eritrea could be destabilizing and further undermine efforts to counter terrorism in the region. 
Prelude to Another Conflict in Tigray 
Almost four years ago, the Ethiopian government and Tigray’s longtime ruling party, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), signed the November 2022 Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (CoHA), stopping one of the deadliest wars of the 21st century. The governments of Ethiopia and Eritrea were aligned in that war against the TPLF, which had been the dominant party in Ethiopia’s ruling coalition from 1991 until 2018, when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power. 
The war divided Ethiopia along ethnic lines, spurring a massive humanitarian crisis, famine, and widespread atrocities. The State Department determined that all parties to the conflict committed war crimes, members of the Ethiopian and Eritrean militaries and allied forces from the Amhara region of Ethiopia committed crimes against humanity, and Amhara forces committed ethnic cleansing in western Tigray. UN human rights experts assessed that Ethiopia’s government and its allies used starvation as a weapon in Tigray and stated that further investigation is needed to determine the possible commission of genocide. A year after the CoHA’s signing, they warned that the human rights situation in Ethiopia remained serious, with conflicts ongoing in other parts of the country and an acute risk of further atrocity crimes. 
Figure 1. Map of Ethiopia
/
Source: CRS graphic. Areas of AFS-related hostilities based on public reporting.
The CoHA was not a comprehensive peace deal. Its signatories committed to cease hostilities, restore constitutional order, form an interim government for Tigray leading to elections, and engage in a political dialogue to resolve their differences. The deal linked the disarming of the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF) to the concurrent withdrawal of foreign and non-federal military forces from Tigray. Eritrea and Amhara forces were not party to the negotiations, however, and the federal government did not enforce their withdrawal. Some Eritrean troops remained, and Amhara forces continued to occupy western Tigray, leaving up to 800,000 people displaced and dependent on dwindling aid. Some reportedly died of starvation in late 2025. 
The TDF began disarming in 2023, but its demobilization was underfunded and stalled in 2025. Meanwhile, a power struggle linked to the CoHA and its selective implementation led Tigray’s pre-war leadership to push for the ouster of the interim government head, Getachew Reda—who had represented the TPLF in the CoHA negotiations—in early 2025. The federal government postponed elections that were expected in 2025 for Tigray, and the election board revoked the TPLF’s party registration. It then recognized other Tigray parties, including a new splinter party led by Getachew, whom Abiy appointed to his cabinet. The TPLF declared that the 2026 elections would not take place in Tigray unless it could compete in them. 
A new armed group, the Tigray Peace Force (TPF), emerged in 2025. Composed of ex-TDF fighters, it vowed to liberate Tigray from the TPLF and clashed with Tigray forces several times. The TPLF accused the government of backing the TPF, including with drone strikes, and of a renewed blockade that restricted fuel, federal funds for public services, and medicines.
The TDF and federal troops clashed directly in early 2026, fueling fears of a return to war as Abiy termed the TPLF “traitors” working to “dismantle Ethiopia” and surged troops to Tigray’s borders. The fighting stopped, but there were signs that both sides were preparing for war, with reports of forced recruitment by both sides. Fighting resumed in early August and escalated, with increasingly frequent drone strikes in Tigray.
Opposition Alliance
On September 20, the TPLF and six other groups announced a new coalition, the Alliance for Survival (AFS). The alliance links disparate groups from seven regions that have pledged to collectively defend themselves “against the devastating war declared upon us”; overthrow Abiy’s “personalist, dictatorial and genocidal regime”; form a transitional government; and hold a dialogue on a new constitution. Among the groups is a faction of the Fano—Amhara militia who rebelled in 2023—and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), which has waged an insurgency since 2018. There has been little media coverage of the ongoing conflicts in Amhara, where the government has reportedly lost control of large areas since 2023, and Oromia (Ethiopia’s most populous region and Abiy’s home area). The government seeks to control the narrative around the conflicts and restricts press coverage of them, per press freedom groups. 
Evolving Conflict
On the day of the AFS statement, a drone hit a convoy carrying U.S. food aid in Tigray. It was one over two dozen airstrikes attributed to the Ethiopian military in Tigray from early August to September 23, when the TPLF, which had reasserted control of Tigray in May, took control of Tigray’s airports and traded blame with federal authorities as heavy fighting unfolded across northern Ethiopia. TPLF forces joined their AFS allies in battles in Afar and Amhara but lost ground to a counteroffensive by the military and government-aligned TPF. The role of Tigrayan fighters in the joint operations against the TPLF has underscored that Tigrayans are divided in the current conflict.  
Ethiopia has expanded its drone arsenal since 2020-2022 war, using drones in its counterinsurgency campaigns in Amhara, Oromia, and, more recently, Tigray. Reported strikes on several military installations across the country suggest the AFS may also have some limited drone capacity. Joint military-TPF operations forced the TPLF to withdraw from Tigray’s capital in early October, and Abiy has since announced a new caretaker government for the region and pledged to hold elections there within six months. The TPLF has rejected the authority, terming it illegitimate. Fighting continues in parts of Tigray, Amhara, Oromia, and Benishangul-Gumuz, home to the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on the Blue Nile River. 
Regional Tensions
The Horn of Africa has a history of border disputes and proxy conflicts. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 that, unresolved, led to reported proxy support. Prime Minister Abiy pursued rapprochement with Eritrea in 2018, and they were allies in the 2020-2022 war. Tensions have risen since 2023, however, and both have cultivated ties with the other’s opposition groups. Abiy began to publicly describe Ethiopia’s lack of sea access as an “existential” matter (it relies on ports in Djibouti and Somalia), and he has referred to its loss of coastline (with Eritrea’s secession) as a historic “mistake.” State media outlets broadcast stories describing Ethiopia’s quest for sea access as a defining national ambition and a strategic imperative. Abiy is rebuilding the country’s navy, with Russian support, and has held military parades hinting at an ambition to reclaim Eritrea’s port of Assab. (Ethiopia has also recently acquired new fighter jets and air defense systems from Russia.) 
Ethiopia’s quest for sovereign sea access spurred tensions with Somalia in 2024. Abiy’s reported offer to recognize the self-declared republic of Somaliland in exchange for coastline on the Gulf of Aden prompted outrage from Somalia. Turkey mediated between the two countries, but the situation led Somalia toward closer ties with Eritrea and Egypt, which has a long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the GERD. Egypt, heavily reliant on the Nile, views the GERD as an existential threat.
Ethiopia’s unfolding conflict overlaps with the war in Sudan, which has been fueled by Middle East rivalries. Sudan’s military-led government accuses Ethiopia of helping the United Arab Emirates (UAE) aid the insurgent Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and enabling drone attacks on Sudan from its territory. Some reports suggest that Ethiopia, a UAE ally, has facilitated RSF supply lines and incursions into Sudan. Ethiopia, for its part, asserts that Sudan has provided support to the TPLF. 
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Egypt, and Sudan of fueling its internal conflicts and in early October broke ties with Eritrea and expelled an Egyptian diplomat. Egypt subsequently hosted a summit with Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia, pushing back on Ethiopia’s positions on the Nile and sea access. Ethiopia has since accused Eritrea of moving troops into Tigray and reportedly hit them with drones. Eritrea denied the allegation and has framed it as a declaration of war. 
U.S. Engagement
The Trump Administration has sought to strengthen relations with Ethiopia and, at the same time, reset long-strained ties with Eritrea. President Trump has also offered to mediate between Ethiopia and Egypt. (His 2020 effort did not resolve the dispute.) U.S. officials describe the relationship with Ethiopia as a “close partnership” and have sought to deepen commercial ties, notably between Boeing and Ethiopian Airlines, Africa’s largest carrier. The Administration has reduced U.S. foreign aid for Ethiopia, including humanitarian assistance for the country.
The Administration moved to terminate Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopia in late 2025, asserting there was “no longer an armed conflict that poses a serious threat to the personal safety of returning Ethiopian nationals.” The Administration has taken since steps to enable security cooperation, waiving security assistance restrictions required under the Child Soldiers Prevention Act (Title IV of P.L. 110-457) based on the government’s reported use of child soldiers and terminating the U.S. arms embargo imposed during the 2020-2022 war. The Administration allowed the Ethiopia-related national emergency established in 2021 to expire in September 2026, ending sanctions imposed on Eritrea’s military and ruling party for their role in the last Tigray war. (No Ethiopians were sanctioned.) 
U.S. official remarks on Ethiopia’s conflict have been limited, but some have called out TPLF leaders, on whom the State Department imposed visa restrictions in June. U.S. officials condemned the September strike on the aid convoy but did not attribute responsibility for it. Officials have urged Ethiopia and Eritrea “to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors” and return to dialogue. Per Secretary Rubio, “The last thing the world needs right now is another war.”

Sexual assault and related offenses are mostly defined and proscribed under state, rather than federal, law. The federal government can act only pursuant to an enumerated power in the Constitution, whereas states have broader authority to enact criminal laws unless otherwise prohibited by the Constitution. Congress has enacted laws prohibiting sexual assault and related conduct, however, where there is a federal jurisdictional basis in the Constitution for Congress to legislate. Congress has also used noncriminal-law means within its jurisdiction, such as grant programs and reporting requirements, to address sex-related crime and its impacts.   
This In Focus discusses selected federal criminal laws related to sexual assault; identifies some of the jurisdictional and evidentiary issues that are commonly analyzed in the context of these laws; highlights other, noncriminal approaches Congress has used to address sexual assault and associated conduct; and closes with considerations for Congress.  
Sexual Assault in Federal Law Generally
“Sexual assault” and other terms describing sex crimes may not have a uniform definition across the country. The Federal Rules of Evidence define “sexual assault” as
a crime under federal law or under state law (as “state” is defined in 18 U.S.C. § 513) involving: 
(1) any conduct prohibited by 18 U.S.C. chapter 109A; 
(2) contact, without consent, between any part of the defendant’s body—or an object—and another person’s genitals or anus; 
(3) contact, without consent, between the defendant’s genitals or anus and any part of another person’s body; 
(4) deriving sexual pleasure or gratification from inflicting death, bodily injury, or physical pain on another person; or 
(5) an attempt or conspiracy to engage in conduct described in subparagraphs (1)–(4).
For purposes of federal law, “sexual assault” is an umbrella term that may cover multiple crimes. One such federal crime, “sexual abuse,” codified at 18 U.S.C. § 2242, generally refers to knowingly engaging in a sex act with another, by way of force or without the consent of the other person, and applies when certain jurisdictional elements (discussed below) are met. Federal law also prohibits aggravated sexual abuse, for example if the alleged victim is subject to certain threats; sexual abuse of a minor involving interstate travel; abuse of an individual in federal custody; statutory rape; and abusive sexual contact, which includes certain intentional touching. 18 U.S.C. § 1153 extends jurisdiction over the aforementioned offenses in “Indian country.” Federal law also prohibits other categories of sex offenses (subject to jurisdictional limitations), including sex trafficking, child pornography, and sexual exploitation of minors.
In addition, Title 18, Chapter 13, contains relevant criminal provisions concerning violations of civil rights. For example, 18 U.S.C. § 242 criminalizes the willful deprivation of a right or privilege protected by the Constitution by individuals acting under the color of law, including through sexual abuse. For example, a state judge who sexually assaulted a party to a case pending before him violated this provision. 18 U.S.C. § 250 enhances the offense level to a felony for violations of Chapter 13 that involve sexual abuse or other sexual misconduct. 
Congress has also criminalized sexual assault in Article 120 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ), the code of military criminal laws governing U.S. military members. These crimes are prosecuted in military courts established under Article I of the Constitution. The UCMJ includes the inchoate offenses of attempt, conspiracy and solicitation for sexual assault crimes.
Jurisdictional Bases
As mentioned above, every legislative act of Congress must be traced to an enumerated power in the Constitution. These powers include governance of federal property and authority over interstate commerce and federal spending, among others. As such, the federal sex offenses described above contain jurisdictional elements limiting their reach in particular ways based on the underlying federal power. For example, the crime of sexual abuse applies only if the underlying offense conduct occurs “in the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States or in a Federal prison, or in any prison, institution, or facility in which persons are held in custody by direction of or pursuant to a contract or agreement with the head of any Federal department or agency.” 
Special Maritime and Territorial Jurisdiction of the United States
Congress has “state-like” authority under a few constitutional provisions to criminalize conduct that occurs in the Special Maritime and Territorial Jurisdiction of the United States (SMTJ), which is statutorily defined to include locations such as the “high seas,” domestic aircrafts in flight, and federal enclaves. 

Other federal criminal laws related to sexual abuse contain the same jurisdictional requirement or rely on different fonts of congressional authority. For example, child pornography crimes demand that the material in question involve a “means or facility” of interstate or foreign commerce, or be “in or affect[]” interstate or foreign commerce. Sex trafficking similarly requires that the trafficking occur “in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce” or within the SMTJ. 
The deprivation of civil rights by individuals acting under color of law is grounded in a different power of Congress: the authority to enforce the Fourteenth Amendment, which generally ensures due process and equal protection of the laws. 
In enacting the sexual assault provisions in Article 120 of the UCMJ, Congress exercised its authority to prescribe rules to govern the military in Article I, Section 8, Clause 14.
Common Evidentiary Issues
As mentioned above, the absence of consent is an element of most sexual assault offenses, including sexual abuse under federal law. Accordingly, the lack of consent is an important and recurring evidentiary issue. The federal sexual abuse statute clarifies that lack of consent requires proof that the alleged victim was either “incapable of appraising the nature of the conduct” or “physically incapable of declining participation in, or communicating unwillingness to engage in, that sexual act.” According to a federal appeals court, “Not all [such courts] ... have decided whether a defendant must know that the victim was incapacitated to be guilty of this offense,” though some courts, including military courts interpreting the UCMJ, require such knowledge.
A person’s impairment due to intoxication may bear on whether that person was capable of providing or communicating consent. As one court concluded, a sexual abuse conviction may be sustained where the alleged victim was awake or had some awareness of the situation but “was physically hampered due to sleep, intoxication, or drug use and thereby rendered physically incapable” of consent. As to sexual acts committed under color of law, the law makes clear that “[c]onsent that is the product of official intimidation, harassment, or coercion is not true consent at all.”
In jurisdictions that require a defendant to know that the alleged victim could not consent to the sex act, a defendant’s intoxication may be relevant to establishing the defendant’s mental state. Federal courts have held, however, that voluntary intoxication is a defense where there is evidence that the defendant was “drunk enough to completely lack the capacity to form the requisite intent,” such as the intent to attempt to commit sexual abuse. 
Selected Noncriminal Federal Laws
Congress also has used its enumerated powers, such as the Spending Clause and the Commerce Clause, to address sexual assault in contexts beyond criminal law. A brief summary of selected statutes in chronological order follows. 
 Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibits sex discrimination in all education programs receiving federal financial assistance. Federal implementing regulations require schools to take steps in responding to sexual harassment allegations, including sexual assault, and to set up grievance procedures for complaints. (For more information on Title IX in this context, see CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11279, Status of Education Department’s Title IX Regulations, by Jared P. Cole (2025).) 
 The Jeanne Clery Campus Safety Act (Clery Act) requires that domestic institutions of higher education participating in Title IV of the Higher Education Act federal student aid programs disclose crime statistics and campus security policies on an annual basis. Such security policies must include procedures for institutional discipline after an incident, such as a sexual assault, has been reported. (For more information on the Clery Act, see CRS In Focus IF12597, The Clery Act, as Amended by the Stop Campus Hazing Act, by Jared P. Cole (2026).) 
 The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) and subsequent reauthorizations enhance legal protections for victims of sexual assault and domestic violence through amendments to existing crimes and the creation of many initiatives, including grant programs and protected housing programs. 34 U.S.C. § 12291(a)(35) defines “sexual assault” for VAWA grant programs as “any nonconsensual sexual act proscribed by Federal, tribal, or State law, including when the victim lacks capacity to consent.”
 The Debbie Smith Act authorizes a grant program for state and local governments designed to enhance their capabilities to process and collect DNA samples in cases involving sexual assault and other violent crime. The Act also contains provisions expanding the information in the Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) and requiring the Federal Bureau of Prisons to take DNA samples from individuals convicted of qualifying federal and District of Columbia offenses.
 The Federal Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA) requires convicted sex offenders to register with the appropriate authority in the jurisdiction of their residence, employment, and school, and contains criminal penalties for noncompliance. (For more information on SORNA, see CRS Report R42692, SORNA: A Legal Analysis of 18 U.S.C. § 2250 (Failure to Register as a Sex Offender), by Charles Doyle (2021).)
Considerations for Congress
As discussed above, Congress has used its legislative authority to criminalize sexual assault within its jurisdiction and to enact laws aimed at facilitating the investigation of sex-related offenses, increasing transparency around these crimes, and preventing recurrence. Congress could pass new laws within its jurisdiction, as it did in enacting legislation in the 119th Congress that requires the Department of Justice to respond to and assess incidents of sexual harassment and sexual assault by incarcerated individuals against prison staff. 
Congress could also consider adjustments to existing laws. For example, legislation introduced in the 119th Congress would increase statutory penalties by amending 18 U.S.C. § 2242 to establish a mandatory minimum prison term for federal sexual abuse offenses. Congress could also consider clarifying language to address nonuniformity among federal appeals courts regarding whether, for purposes of federal crimes involving alleged absence of consent, a defendant must know that the alleged victim is incapable of providing or communicating consent.

api_metadata.summary:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressed rapidly in recent years, driven by rapid advances in large language models (LLMs). AI has led to a surge in business borrowing and investment in data centers, semiconductors, and other physical capital spending and has fueled a surge in related stock prices. As a result, investment in AI has been a significant source of economic growth in recent quarters. While a recent boon to the economy, AI investment has likely also put upward pressure on inflation, interest rates, and imports, slowing other parts of the economy. Further, if AI investment proves to be a bubble that subsequently bursts, it could be destabilizing for the economy. 
Contribution to Economic Growth
One of the main ways in which AI has impacted the economy is in its effects on output, as measured by gross domestic product (GDP). GDP accounts for all expenditures within the economy, including businesses’ investment in the plant (e.g., data centers), equipment (e.g., hardware), and intellectual property (e.g., software and research) needed to build AI. 
The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) does not a produce a specific line item for “AI investment” or similar category within GDP data. Therefore, estimates use proxy categories to account for AI investment, such as expenditures on computer equipment, software, or data center construction. Methodologies differ and likely either over- or underestimate the impact of AI investment, depending on their treatment of potential proxy categories, data centers, and imports, among other possible differences. On the one hand, estimates will be too high when categories include similar spending that is not AI related: For example, not all semiconductors are used for AI. On the other hand, a focus on AI investment is too narrow to fully capture AI’s effects on growth: For example, it would not include growth in value added for non-AI firms attributable to those firms’ spending on AI services. 
Many aspects of AI investment in the economy currently rely on imports, as much of the hardware that is used to build data centers is produced abroad. For example, Federal Reserve researchers estimated that global trade in AI-related products (servers, graphics cards, and related parts) increased 65% in the first half of 2025 compared to the first half of 2024. GDP is calculated by subtracting imports. Therefore, capital expenditures related to the AI build-out are larger than the effect of the build-out on overall GDP growth. Figure 1 shows that AI capital expenditures have increased noticeably since the first quarter of 2025 but so have AI imports, resulting in a more modest acceleration of AI’s contribution to GDP growth, as estimated by the Federal Reserve.
In addition to its effects on GDP, AI also affects productivity and the labor market, which indirectly affects economic growth in ways that are not directly measured and are harder to estimate. AI has been shown, in some cases, to improve task and worker productivity and potentially spur further innovation that begets more productivity growth. Potential impacts on the labor market are more uncertain, with the potential for some redistribution of jobs, as well as a potential further shift of the share of income from labor to capital. For more information, see CRS In Focus IF12762, The Macroeconomic Effects of Artificial Intelligence, by Lida R. Weinstock and Paul Tierno.
Figure 1. Investment and Net Exports Related to AI
/
Source: CRS using Federal Reserve estimates.
Potential Risks
While AI has undoubtedly been an engine of economic growth in the United States in recent years, it carries risks to the economy, including that AI investment is a bubble that could burst, could raise inflation, or could raise interest rates.
That the AI build-out has been a large driver of growth begets questions for economists and policymakers that do not have straightforward answers—is economic growth currently unbalanced and overly dependent on AI? So far, AI’s contribution to growth has not been large enough to significantly change the overall growth picture; however, AI’s contribution to growth was more significant in 2025 and the first quarter of 2026 than in previous years (see Figure 2). Additionally, Figure 2 could understate AI’s contribution to growth because it does not consider any multiplier effect that occurs when businesses and individuals spend income that they received from AI purchasers.
On the other hand, Figure 2 may also overstate AI investment’s effects on growth since it may also be increasing inflation, interest rates, and imports, thereby crowding out other economic activity. In other words, other parts of the economy would grow more rapidly in the absence of the AI investment boom. 
Interest Rates and the Current Account Deficit
A great deal of the AI build-out is being funded by debt. This amount of borrowing could increase overall interest rates and the current account deficit (colloquially, the “trade deficit”) in turn. In economic parlance, investment must be financed with saving, and therefore if domestic saving is insufficient, foreign saving must make up the difference. This net inflow of foreign capital results in a current account deficit. Although the deficit has increased somewhat during the AI investment boom, Federal Reserve Bank of New York research attributes this to the larger government budget deficit, finding business saving and investment rates relatively unchanged, with higher AI investment offset by a decline in other business investment.
Figure 2. AI Contribution to GDP Growth
/
Source: CRS using Bureau of Economic Analysis and Federal Reserve estimates.
Notes: This figure shows only one estimate of AI investment’s contribution to growth. Other sources will yield different results. Bars indicate percentage points; the solid line indicates percentages.
Other business investment may be falling because this large amount of debt issuance has increased demand for capital and is thus likely also contributing to the increase in long-term interest rates throughout the economy, raising financing costs for businesses, households (e.g., through higher mortgage rates), and the government. This increase in rates make U.S. investments relatively more attractive to foreigners, resulting in a larger current account deficit. 
Inflation
AI investment may be contributing to near-term price pressures as demand for AI-related goods such as chips has increased, potentially causing bottlenecks that cause their prices to increase. Data centers may also contribute to increases in the demand for, and therefore price of, electricity. Goldman Sachs estimates these factors will cause inflation to rise by 0.5 percentage points at its peak. To avoid this causing an increase in overall inflation, other prices would need to fall, either because AI allows other goods to be produced more inexpensively or because fiscal or monetary policy is tightened to reduce overall demand. To date, tightening has been modest, and policymakers have not successfully reduced inflation to the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. These factors, while affecting inflation in the short term, would not be expected to continue to do so in the medium term, at which point AI’s inflationary effects would be more dependent on the extent of productivity gains seen from its dissemination and use, for example.
The 119th Congress has shown interest in these issues. For example, the Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340) would require state utility regulators to consider standards to hold “large-load” customers responsible for higher energy costs. The bill passed the House, but a cloture vote failed in the Senate.
Investment Bubble
If AI investment and growth is sustainable, its effects on the growth of the rest of the economy may be acceptable for the economy as a whole—throughout history, new technologies have crowded out less advanced industries. But if there is an AI investment bubble, that bubble could burst and cause significant harm to the economy—especially if other parts of the economy could not generate growth to pick up the slack. The AI industry has a few characteristics that could make it prone to a bubble, meaning that the actual and planned level of AI investment will not ultimately prove to be financially viable: 
AI requires large physical capital spending to make further improvements, and that capital depreciates rapidly.
Revenues are currently small relative to investment spending but are projected to grow rapidly.
AI is a general-purpose technology, which could have unforeseeable applications across many industries, so plausible projections of future AI demand vary greatly.
The AI build-out is financed by a large amount of debt.
Projected revenue growth has led to high equity valuations for leading AI firms.
There may be a “winner takes all” aspect of the industry, in which a small number of firms may end up capturing most of the market share—and the rest may go out of business.
AI investment sometimes involves “circular financing,” (financing is between AI-centric companies that also do business with one another), which may be artificially increasing demand.
Together, these factors carry a risk that if future AI revenues do not grow at their rapid projected pace for some or all of the leading firms, current AI investment spending will prove to have been a bubble that could subsequently burst, leading to a devaluation of AI firms’ equity, debt, and capital assets. In that case, equity and debt holders could be exposed to large and unexpected losses, including through bankruptcy or default. The magnitude of potential losses could decrease economic growth through reduced investment spending and reduced consumption via a wealth effect (as investors bearing losses reduced their consumption spending in response) and might cause financial instability, with spillovers to the global economy. 
Financial bubbles are difficult to accurately identify ahead of time, and an AI bubble’s existence is hotly contested between skeptics and optimists. For example, a Bank for International Settlements working paper questions the sustainability of the AI boom, estimating overinvestment of 1.5 times the efficient level. Losses are expected to be greater as debt grows.
Despite these potential warning signs, many believe that the AI investment boom is likely to continue for now, suggesting that there is investor confidence in AI’s prospects. For example, Goldman Sachs predicts “robust” short-term growth, with AI investment increasing to 2.8% of GDP in 2028, which is consistent with past technology build-outs.

The Department of the Interior’s (DOI’s) Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) and Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) share responsibility for managing the nation’s ocean energy resources on about 3.2 billion acres of the U.S. outer continental shelf (OCS). In July 2026, the Secretary of the Interior issued an order for the merger of BOEM and BSEE into a new Marine Minerals Administration (MMA), combining BOEM’s role of administering offshore energy and mineral leasing with BSEE’s role of overseeing offshore safety and environmental protection. A separate DOI office, the Office of Natural Resources Revenue (ONRR), manages public revenues from federal offshore and onshore energy projects. All these DOI entities receive appropriations in annual Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies appropriations acts. Issues for Congress include determining the aggregate and program-level appropriations for each entity. 
On June 5, 2026, the House Appropriations Committee reported H.R. 9171 (H.Rept. 119-687), with FY2027 funding for BOEM, BSEE, and ONRR. (DOI had submitted a budget request for a combined MMA, but H.R. 9171 contains separate appropriations for BOEM and BSEE.) FY2027 appropriations were not enacted by the start of the fiscal year. A continuing resolution, P.L. 119-103, Division A, generally provides continuing appropriations for DOI agencies and offices through December 11, 2026, unless other appropriations are enacted earlier. 
Total budget authority for BOEM and BSEE includes both discretionary appropriations and offsetting collections derived from a portion of OCS rental receipts, cost-recovery fees, and (for BSEE) inspection fees. The discretionary appropriations for each fiscal year are reduced by the amount of eligible receipts and fees collected, so that the final amount appropriated to each agency is the net of those collections. Discussions of account- and activity-level funding in the sections below refer to total budget authority, regardless of offsets. ONRR’s funding does not include offsetting collections.
MMA Budget Request
The Trump Administration requested $296.2 million in total budget authority for MMA for FY2027 (Table 1). The request combined accounts and activities that in FY2026 and previous years were attributed separately to BOEM and BSEE. Also, the Administration proposed legislative language allowing for the transfer of program funds to “effectuate” the MMA reorganization. The FY2027 request for MMA was 27% lower than the combined FY2026 budget authority of $403.0 million for BOEM and BSEE provided in P.L. 119-74, Division C. 
The budget request sought appropriations for two main MMA accounts. Within the primary account (called the MMA account), it is not always clear how specified budget activities correspond to FY2026 funding for BOEM and BSEE as separate agencies. The Administration requested $186.2 million for Conventional Energy Operations. This activity would fund oil and gas leasing and development, such as development of the five-year oil and gas leasing program administered by BOEM. It would also fund functions like OCS facility inspections that are typically performed by BSEE. Based on “notional” comparisons, “had BOEM and BSEE been unified,” the Administration estimated that the FY2026 funding for this activity was $234.9 million. The requested FY2027 decrease reflects the proposed elimination of BSEE’s renewable energy program as well as staff consolidation.
For the Marine Minerals budget activity, the Administration requested $17.8 million to fund OCS critical mineral lease sales, post-sale activities, assessments of critical mineral resources, and collection of baseline environmental data. For FY2026, BOEM’s Marine Minerals activity received $13.8 million. (BSEE had no marine minerals funding in FY2026.) The requested increase would support holding three anticipated lease sales—the first such sales on the OCS—and preparing for future sales (e.g., off Virginia). The budget request also included a legislative proposal to share federal marine mineral revenues with states and the Land and Water Conservation Fund (54 U.S.C. §§200301 et seq.).Table 1. The Administration requested $52.5 million for Environmental Programs and Enforcement, supporting environmental studies and assessments such as those required by the National Environmental Policy Act (42 U.S.C. §§4321 et seq.), as well as environmental enforcement activities like offshore facility inspections and related activities. The supported activities would include both BOEM and BSEE functions. The Administration estimated comparable FY2026 appropriations at $78.7 million. The requested decrease reflects staff consolidation.
Funding of $30.2 million was requested for Executive Direction, to support leadership and management functions such as budgeting, communications, and others. Both BOEM and BSEE functions are included, and the Administration estimated combined FY2026 funding at $37.5 million. The requested decrease reflects staff consolidation.
The FY2027 request did not include funding in the MMA account for two budget activities that had been funded in FY2026. The Administration proposed to eliminate the Renewable Energy budget activity (for which FY2026 funding was shown as $20.0 million through BOEM) “in alignment” with Executive Order 14154. Required work on existing offshore wind leases would be supported through the Conventional Energy Operations activity. The budget request also included a legislative proposal to impose inspection fees for offshore wind facilities. Also, the Administration proposed to eliminate the Offshore Decommissioning budget activity (funded through BSEE at $2.9 million for FY2026), stating that decommissioning of infrastructure orphaned by bankrupt operators can be achieved using prior appropriations. In connection with a regulatory proposal to set toppling in place as the default standard for offshore oil and gas infrastructure decommissioning, the Administration included a legislative proposal for a “Topple-in-Place Contingency Fund,” which would be an industry-supported fund to address damage to fishing gear from toppled wells and to address federal liabilities from orphaned infrastructure. 
Separate from the MMA account, the Administration requested $9.5 million for the Oil Spill Research account, corresponding to BSEE’s account with this title funded at $15.1 million for FY2026. This account funds research and planning for oil spill response and supports Ohmsett, the National Oil Spill Response Research and Renewable Energy Test Facility. 
ONRR Budget Request 
ONRR is funded under the broader appropriation for DOI’s Department-Wide Programs. For FY2027, the Administration requested $134.1 million for ONRR, a 16% decrease from the FY2026 funding of $159.9 million (Table 1). The requested decrease reflects “efficiency” gains and the completion of an information technology modernization project, according to the Administration.
House Committee-Approved H.R. 9171
H.R. 9171 would provide $392.3 million in total FY2027 budget authority for BOEM and BSEE combined, consisting of $182.9 million for BOEM and $209.4 million for BSEE (Table 1). Although DOI had requested legislative language allowing funding transfers to facilitate the MMA merger, H.R. 9171 does not contain such language and provides separate funding for BOEM and BSEE. The combined total for the two agencies is 3% less than enacted for FY2026 and 32% more than the request. 
BOEM’s funding is contained in a single budget account, Ocean Energy Management. Within this account, H.Rept. 119-687, the committee report, specifies $73.0 million for Conventional Energy (compared to $70.2 million for FY2026), $5.0 million for Renewable Energy ($20.0 million FY2026), $73.1 million for Environmental Assessment (level with FY2026), $17.8 million for Marine Minerals ($13.8 million FY2026), and $14.0 million for Executive Direction (level with FY2026). With respect to Renewable Energy, H.Rept. 119-687 states that the recommended $5.0 million is for “priorities of the Department of the Interior” and is “intended to be consistent” with President Trump’s January 2025 memorandum temporarily withdrawing the OCS from renewable energy leasing and requiring a review of federal wind leasing and permitting practices. 
H.R. 9171 would provide BSEE funding in two accounts: Offshore Safety and Environmental Enforcement (OSEE) and Oil Spill Research (OSR). Within OSEE, H.Rept. 119-687 specifies $155.0 million for Operations, Safety and Regulation (compared to $156.8 million for FY2026), $5.0 million for Environmental Enforcement ($5.6 million FY2026), $15.5 million for Administrative Operations (level with FY2026), $15.9 million for Executive Direction (level with FY2026), and $2.9 million for Offshore Decommissioning (level with FY2026). In the OSR account, the Oil Spill Research activity would be funded at $15.1 million (level with FY2026). 
Regarding offshore decommissioning, H.Rept. 119-687 expresses the committee’s ongoing support for the Rigs-to-Reefs program and encourages BSEE to utilize and promote the program. H.R. 9171 does not contain the Administration’s requested legislative language to establish a contingency fund for offshore infrastructure toppled in place as part of this program. Separately, similar to prior annual appropriations acts, H.R. 9171 contains general provisions imposing fees for inspections of offshore oil and gas facilities. The bill also includes provisions requested by DOI to impose new fees for inspections of offshore wind facilities. Regarding the latter, H.Rept. 119-687 states that the committee “expects the Agency to ensure that such fees are fair, transparent, and commensurate with the actual cost of inspection activities,” and directs BSEE to report to the committee with a detailed basis for the wind inspection fees.  
Net Appropriations
Net of estimated offsetting collections of $135.2 million, MMA’s request in its FY2027 budget justification was $160.9 million. Using a different estimate of offsetting collections ($154.0 million), H.Rept. 119-687 shows a net request of $142.2 million for MMA (Table 1). H.R. 9171 would provide net appropriations of $237.3 million for BOEM and BSEE combined, 15% less than FY2026. Using the net request as reported in H.Rept. 119-687 ($142.2 million), H.R. 9171 would provide 67% more than requested in net appropriations.

This Insight describes federal online resources intended to help students and parents plan and acquire funds for postsecondary education. These include federal resources that provide general information on scholarships, grants, fellowships, loans, and internships for undergraduate and graduate students; federal student aid (FSA) programs administered by the U.S. Department of Education (ED); and funding particular to specific education disciplines and categories of students. Some resources contain information on the repayment, forgiveness, and discharge of educational debt. 
Since January 2025, President Trump has issued executive orders (E.O.s) that have addressed the use of federal funds in various areas. Several of these executive orders, aspects of which are subject to litigation, direct relevant agencies to pause certain grant-related and other funding activities and may affect the resources discussed in this Insight.
Some websites and programs referenced in this Insight may be undergoing changes or be inaccessible as agencies comply with recent executive orders. If you are unable to access a reference, please contact CRS.
General Resources
The following websites provide planning tools for pursuing postsecondary education, including financial aid information and information on planning for and developing skills for careers.
U.S. Department of Education
The Federal Student Aid portal helps students learn about how financial aid administered by ED works, the types of assistance, and how to apply for financial aid through the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) and establish an individual FSA account. The portal provides links to websites with information on how aid is calculated, tips for comparing school aid offers, and how to accept financial aid. Students also can learn about repaying loans, consolidating loans, applying for loan forgiveness programs, and avoiding default. 
College Affordability and Transparency Center (CATC) provides a one-stop site of tools for parents and students to compare colleges and their tuition and fees, net prices, and costs. 
College Scorecard is a comparison tool for information on school sizes, settings, graduation rates, average costs, and salary ranges per field of study. 
CollegeNavigator is a search tool for individual school data and for creating lists of schools by size, setting, selectivity, degree programs, location, institution type, religious affiliation, and other categories.
Net Price Calculator Center—Search for Schools’ Calculator is a search tool for institutions’ net price calculators, which allows undergraduate students to calculate an estimated net price of attendance at an institution (defined as cost of attendance minus grant and scholarship aid) based on what similar students paid in a previous year. Individuals may also contact the postsecondary institution directly if they have questions about a specific net price calculator. 
The Knowledge Center portal provides guidance, resources, and information related to the administration and processing of financial aid programs for postsecondary students authorized under Title IV of the Higher Education Act (HEA). Title IV of the HEA authorizes funding through grants and loans to students. Although designed for financial aid administrators, the website includes detailed information on rules for federal student aid, including the Federal Student Aid Handbook. 
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s Paying for College website provides information on making informed financial decisions about how to pay for college. It includes financial guides for understanding student loans and repayment options and for managing money while in college, such as choosing a bank account and the impact of financial aid disbursement on financial accounts.
U.S. Department of the Treasury
Internal Revenue Service (IRS)—Tax Benefits for Education: Information Center provides an overview on tax credits, deductions, and savings plans to help taxpayers with their higher education expenses. The center also links to the IRS’s Interactive Tax Assistant tool to help determine eligibility for educational credits or deductions. 
U.S. Department of Labor
The U.S. Department of Labor’s CareerOneStop GetMyFuture provides a one-stop site of tools targeted to individuals aged 14 to 24 to help them explore careers, learn about and locate training or education programs, and conduct a job search. 
CareerOneStop Scholarship Finder is a search tool for scholarships, fellowships, loans, and other financial aid opportunities. Users can search by keyword or by category (e.g., award type, residence preferences, and study level). The information is provided under a third-party license and includes nonfederal resources.
CareerOneStop Explore Careers provides information tools for identifying, planning, and developing skills for careers.
Apprenticeship.gov provides career seekers, employers, and educators information on apprenticeship opportunities by type of industry, Department of Labor- and industry-recognized apprenticeship programs, and state tuition support initiatives.
Federal Trade Commission
The Federal Trade Commission’s (FTC’s) Education and Training website provides an overview on avoiding educational scams by providing tips on choosing a college or vocational school, paying for school, avoiding fake degrees, and other scams. It includes information on how to report financial aid, scholarship, and student loan scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and the individual’s state attorney general.
Resources for Specific Purposes or Populations
The following resources, organized by federal agency, provide information on college and career planning for specialized educational disciplines (e.g., international studies, health) and categories of students (e.g., veterans, military personnel, and dependents).
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
Education & Training Opportunities serves as a portal to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ education and training opportunities for health professionals and students, including programs that support health care providers and researchers.  
Health Resources and Services Administration Loans & Scholarships provides links to scholarships and loan repayment programs, such as the Native Hawaiian Health Scholarship, National Health Service Corps (scholarship or loan repayment), and Nurse Corps (scholarship or loan repayment).
U.S. Department of State
Student Resources provides a portal to a broad range of State Department educational resources.
Exchange Programs for U.S. Citizens provides resources on undergraduate and graduate exchange experiences, travel and living arrangements, and finding programs.
USA Study Abroad provides resources on study abroad programs for U.S. citizens who are high school, undergraduate, and graduate students. See Foreign Government Scholarships applicable to U.S. students.
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
Veterans Administration’s Education and Training Benefits website provides information on education benefits available to honorably discharged veterans and servicemembers (including reservists and National Guard members) and educational assistance for survivors and dependents.

api_metadata.summary:
The Healthy Start program (42 U.S.C. §254c-8) aims to improve health outcomes before, during, and after pregnancy. The program funds projects in geographic areas with high infant mortality rates (IMRs) and other adverse perinatal outcomes (see Figure 1 for recent trends in the national IMR compared with Healthy Start sites). Healthy Start emphasizes flexibility in meeting family- and community-specific needs and funds local organizations to provide tailored health and social services to women, their partners, infants, and children (up to 18 months). The program also funds the Healthy Start Technical Assistance and Support Center, which provides training, resources, and support to grantees.
Healthy Start has historically been administered by the Maternal and Child Health Bureau within the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS); the extent to which the HHS restructuring plan might affect the program is unclear. Healthy Start is statutorily authorized through FY2025; however, the program’s funding has been provided through appropriations laws, most recently through December 11, 2026.
Overview
Healthy Start was established in 1991 as part of a presidential initiative to decrease IMRs. The pilot program funded 15 community-based sites where IMRs were 1.5 to 2.0 times higher than the national average. Grantees were tasked with identifying and developing community-based approaches to reduce IMRs and improve the health and well-being of women, infants, children, and families; such services included case management, outreach, and health education, among others. The Children’s Health Act of 2000 (P.L. 106-310) codified, and authorized appropriations through FY2005 for, the program. The Healthy Start Reauthorization Act of 2007 (P.L. 110-339) reauthorized appropriations through FY2013 and added additional grant requirements. The Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act (P.L. 116-136) reauthorized appropriations through FY2025 and added evaluation requirements (including a U.S. Government Accountability Office [GAO] report discussed below), among other amendments. Recent funding is presented in Table 1.

In FY2024, the program funded a cohort of 115 grantees across 37 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico. In addition to the services discussed above, grantees provide clinical services that may include prenatal, postnatal, or mental health care; screening and referral services; and peer support, provider training, and other social services. New to the FY2024 cohort, all grantees must offer group prenatal health and parenting education services. Each Healthy Start project has a Community Consortium composed of community members and is required to coordinate services with agencies administering the Title V State Maternal and Child Health Block Grant program. 
Healthy Start has also provided supplemental grants aimed at training doulas, addressing infant health disparities through other determinants of health, and developing innovative care models. Congress has at times directed supplemental funding to Healthy Start to respond to emerging issues, such as childhood lead exposure during the Flint water crisis (P.L. 114-322; P.L. 114-254). Most recently, Healthy Start’s pilot program to address high blood pressure during pregnancy received targeted FY2025 appropriations.

Program Evaluations and Policy Debates
Healthy Start has undergone multiple program evaluations since its inception. The most recent national   evaluation in 2017 used a multimethod and multiyear approach to examine outcomes among Healthy Start participants compared with nonparticipants. Using program data, vital records, and other surveillance data, the evaluation indicated Healthy Start participants were more likely than nonparticipants to receive early and more frequent prenatal care, have lower rates of low birthweight infants, and implement safe sleep practices. However, many participants did not reach program targets related to breastfeeding and screenings for intimate partner violence. In 2024, a congressionally directed GAO report recommended that HRSA implement documented processes for reviewing program evaluation data and coordinating with other programs. According to GAO, HHS has partially addressed both recommendations. HRSA also initiated a national Healthy Start evaluation in 2021, which is expected to be published in late 2026.
Some observers assert that Healthy Start is duplicative with the Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting program, while others contend that it is distinct, noting shared goals but differences in grantees, services provided, statutory authorities, and other requirements. The aforementioned 2024 GAO report also discussed similarities and differences in strategies, target populations, and services offered by related programs. Reflecting this debate, in recent years, some appropriations proposals have sought to eliminate funding for Healthy Start (e.g., H.Rept. 118-585; H.Rept. 119-271), while others have sought to continue, or in some cases expand, the program (e.g., S.Rept. 118-207; S.Rept. 119-55).  The program was proposed for elimination in both the FY2026 and FY2027 presidential budget requests. 
Policy Considerations
Two bills in the 119th Congress aim to reauthorize Healthy Start. H.R. 3302 would authorize $145 million in annual appropriations for each of FY2026 through FY2030; S. 3799 (as reported) would authorize the same total for each of FY2027 through FY2031. Aside from these proposals, Congress could reauthorize the program at the same, increased, or decreased funding levels; alter program requirements; or direct supplemental inquiries into specific health or program outcomes. Congress may also consider examining forthcoming evaluation data or recent IMR trends to understand program impact, take no action to continue the program, or pursue other considerations.

The second Trump Administration has proposed to develop a “next-generation missile defense shield” against nuclear and conventional attacks that it has called a “Golden Dome for America.” Since the 1950s, Members of Congress have periodically debated the costs, feasibility, scope, and sufficiency of strategic defense systems that could limit damage to the U.S. homeland from a nuclear attack. In these debates, some Members have stated that some of these systems could adversely affect U.S. security by destabilizing nuclear deterrence relationships with adversaries and/or by contributing to a competition in nuclear-armed missiles. This Insight focuses on certain strategic stability issues that Congress may consider when providing oversight of or funding for Golden Dome. See the text box for a definition of strategic stability.
Strategic Stability
A state of relations between adversarial nuclear-armed states where neither side has an incentive to (1) employ nuclear weapons first (known as crisis stability or first strike stability) or (2) build up nuclear weapons (known as arms race stability). 

Background
One of the major roles of U.S. strategic nuclear forces has been and remains the deterrence of a nuclear attack on the U.S. homeland through a threat of nuclear retaliation (a second strike). After the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, the United States and the Soviet Union gradually sought to improve strategic stability in their mutual deterrence relationship. The Johnson and Nixon Administrations concluded that deploying missile defenses (anti-ballistic missile, or ABM, systems) against a large-scale Soviet nuclear attack was infeasible and that U.S. interests would be better served by negotiating with the Soviet Union to reduce Soviet incentives for a nuclear first strike or an offensive nuclear missile buildup to overcome U.S. ABM systems. In 1972, after hearings, the Senate voted 88-2 to provide advice and consent to ratification of the ABM Treaty that restricted the development and deployment of ABM systems and approved an Interim Agreement that imposed numerical limits on strategic nuclear ballistic missiles. 
As part of his 1983 Strategic Defense Initiative, President Ronald Reagan articulated a shift in U.S. strategy from threatening nuclear retaliation toward a defensive approach reliant on intercepting Soviet strategic ballistic missiles with space-based ABM systems. In negotiations that eventually led to the 1991 Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START I), Soviet leaders sought to keep the United States in the ABM Treaty and limit U.S. space-based ABM systems.
Ballistic Missile Defenses in U.S.-Russian Relations
After the end of the Cold War, Congress passed several Missile Defense Acts setting policy and providing funding for missile defenses to protect the U.S. homeland from threats posed by the regional proliferation of missile technologies. Russian concerns about these efforts complicated bilateral nuclear arms control during the 1990s. However, the United States and Russia concluded the 2002 Moscow Treaty that further reduced strategic nuclear forces despite the concomitant U.S. withdrawal from the ABM Treaty. During the Clinton, George W. Bush, and Obama Administrations, the two countries also attempted to cooperate bilaterally and within the NATO-Russia framework on elements of a collaborative missile defense system.
Russian officials express concern that U.S. missile defenses are not limited programs aimed at countering regional threats like North Korea or Iran but are instead an open-ended effort aimed at undermining Russia’s ability to engage in nuclear retaliation. Russian negotiators unsuccessfully sought “legally binding guarantees” that U.S. missile defenses would not be aimed against Russian strategic nuclear forces. The 2010 New START Treaty’s preamble included language, secured by Russian negotiators, regarding an “interrelationship” between strategic offenses and defenses. The Senate’s resolution of advice and consent to New START ratification stated that the treaty did not restrict U.S. missile defenses. 
The Russian military has some missile defense systems and capabilities to protect its nuclear deterrent, as well as to counter U.S. missile defenses beyond traditional countermeasures. In 2018, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced that Russia had novel nuclear weapons to counter U.S. missile defenses. During the Biden Administration, Russian officials focused on missile defense as one of the factors, in addition to nuclear weapons and conventional precision strike, affecting strategic stability. 
U.S. missile defense policy has become an area of coordination for Russia and the People’s Republic of China (PRC), whose growing nuclear arsenal now poses “a direct threat to the [U.S.] Homeland,” according to U.S. intelligence estimates. In a May 2025 statement, Russia and the PRC stated that, through Golden Dome, the United States sought to undermine their ability to engage in nuclear retaliation. 
Potential Strategic Stability Considerations 
As Congress assesses the Trump Administration’s homeland missile defense plans and their strategic stability implications, it may consider the following issues:
What are the implications of Golden Dome for U.S. nuclear deterrence strategy, particularly in an emerging environment of two nuclear peers? Through executive branch briefings, hearings, and other oversight activities, Congress may question Administration approaches to this issue in the context of Administration reviews of nuclear and missile defense policies and postures. In defense authorization and appropriation legislation, Congress may provide policy direction and funding for limited or expansive approaches to Golden Dome—decisions that may involve making budgetary tradeoffs among defense programs.  
How might Russia and the PRC respond to Golden Dome and on what timeline? Through intelligence community briefings, Congress may track Russian and PRC changes to their nuclear forces, their development of countermeasures, and the evolution of their doctrines and operational concepts in response to Golden Dome. Congress may also evaluate existing reporting requirements on nuclear cooperation between Russia and the PRC (e.g., P.L. 118-31, §1649) and determine whether the requirements should be amended to include cooperation or coordination between Russia and the PRC on missile defenses and counterspace issues. 
What is the relationship between Golden Dome and U.S. arms control with Russia and the PRC? President Donald Trump has expressed interest in engaging with Russia and the PRC on nuclear arms control issues. Through executive branch briefings, hearings, and other oversight activities, Congress may seek to understand Administration views on this issue, as well as assess the implications of arms control for U.S. nuclear deterrence strategy and nuclear and missile defense policies, programs, and postures.
